checked: Researched from state constitutions, laws and historians (two researchers, 30 Oct 2026), then fact-checked independently: 71 quotes checked, 67 verbatim; no disagreements on the three classes except North Carolina's rule for white men (marked unsure in its text). Version 1.1.0 (30 Oct 2026): wording corrected after a fact-check of the lesson (Virginia 1830, New York 1821, South Carolina and Tennessee led with 'no property was needed', Connecticut's tax route first, no 'text wasn't checked').

whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
blackMen: Only with extra rules, or kept out in practice

women: Women could not vote in any state in 1828; New Jersey ended women's voting in 1807.

states.electorMethod: Voters, by districts, with two electors chosen statewide (state resolve of 1828).
states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule; paupers could not vote (Constitution of 1820).
states.blackMenRule: Could vote on the same terms as white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1820, Art. II

states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule since 1792; paupers could not vote (Constitution of 1792).
states.blackMenRule: Could vote on the same terms as white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1792

states.electorMethod: Voters, statewide, for the first time (the legislature chose in 1824).
states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule (Constitution of 1793).
states.blackMenRule: Could vote on the same terms as white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1793, Ch. II, sec. 21 (Vermont State Archives)

states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to have paid a state or county tax within two years (1821 amendment, which ended the property rule).
states.blackMenRule: Could vote on the same terms as white men.
states.source: Amendment of 1821, Art. III

states.whiteMenRule: Had to own land worth $134, or be the eldest son of a man who did (rules from colonial times, kept until 1842).
states.blackMenRule: Shut out by a state law of 1822 (from historians' accounts; the text of the law wasn't found).
states.source: Rhode Island Historical Society; Providence College Dorr Rebellion project

states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to have paid a state tax within the year, or served a year in the militia, or own land worth $7 a year (Constitution of 1818).
states.blackMenRule: Shut out by a state law of 1814, then by the Constitution of 1818, which allowed only white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1818, Art. VI, sec. 2 (Connecticut Secretary of the State)

states.electorMethod: Voters, by districts; the district electors then chose two more (McPherson v. Blacker, 1892).
states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule since an 1826 amendment; the 1821 constitution had already eased the rules for white men.
states.blackMen: Only with extra rules, or kept out in practice
states.blackMenRule: The 1821 constitution set a new rule for Black men only: own property worth $250, pay tax on it, and have been a citizen for three years. In 1825 only 298 Black men in the whole state qualified.
states.source: Constitution of 1821, Art. II, sec. 1, and the 1826 amendment; Peter J. Galie, Albany Law Review (the 298 figure)

states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: The law still named property, but in practice men who paid a tax could vote (act of 1807, as historians describe its use).
states.blackMenRule: Shut out, with women, by a state law of 1807, which allowed only free white men.
states.source: Voter qualification law of 1807; National Park Service

states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to have paid a state or county tax within two years; sons of voters aged 21 or 22 were excused (Constitution of 1790).
states.blackMen: Only with extra rules, or kept out in practice
states.blackMenRule: The constitution didn't mention race, but in many places, Philadelphia among them, officials kept Black men from voting. A new constitution shut them out in 1838.
states.source: Constitution of 1790, Art. III, sec. 1

states.electorMethod: The state legislature; voters had no direct say in choosing the president's electors.
states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to have paid a state or county tax. This rule was for state elections.
states.blackMenRule: Allowed only white men (Constitution of 1792, as quoted in a Delaware archives document).
states.source: American Presidency Project (1828 election); Delaware Public Archives

states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule since 1810.
states.blackMenRule: Shut out by a law of 1801, confirmed in 1810, which allowed only free white men.
states.source: Laws of Maryland (Archives of Maryland), and Keyssar, The Right to Vote

states.whiteMenRule: Had to own 25 acres with a house, 50 acres of unimproved land, or a town lot with a house (law of 1785). A new constitution in 1830 loosened the rule.
states.blackMenRule: The 1785 law excluded "free negroes or mulattoes".
states.source: Act of 1785 (Hening, Statutes at Large, vol. 12)

states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Voters for the state House of Commons had to have paid public taxes; voters for the state Senate had to own 50 acres. Which rule applied to electors isn't confirmed.
states.blackMenRule: Could vote until 1835, when the state shut them out.
states.source: Constitution of 1776, Arts. VII and VIII; NCpedia

states.electorMethod: The state legislature, as it did until 1860; voters had no direct say in choosing the president's electors.
states.whiteMenRule: No property was needed: owning 50 acres or a town lot, or living in the district six months, was enough (1810 amendment). This rule was for state elections.
states.blackMenRule: The constitution allowed only free white men (Constitution of 1790).
states.source: American Presidency Project; South Carolina Encyclopedia

states.electorMethod: Voters, statewide, for the first time (the legislature chose in 1824).
states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to have paid all taxes due (Constitution of 1798).
states.blackMenRule: Free Black men were not treated as citizens, so they could not vote; the clause itself doesn't say white.
states.source: Constitution of 1798, Art. IV, sec. 1; Cooper v. Savannah (1848)

states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule; voters voted aloud, not on paper (Constitution of 1799).
states.blackMenRule: Shut out by the Constitution of 1799.
states.source: Kentucky Secretary of State, constitutional history

states.whiteMenRule: No property was needed: owning land in the county, or living there six months, was enough (Constitution of 1796).
states.blackMenRule: Could vote until 1834, when a new constitution shut them out.
states.source: Constitution of 1796, Art. III, sec. 1

states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to have paid a state or county tax, or worked on the public roads (Constitution of 1802).
states.blackMenRule: The Constitution of 1802 allowed only white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1802, Art. IV (transcription)

states.electorMethod: Voters, statewide (a law of 1824 set this; one 1892 court opinion says by districts).
states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule (Constitution of 1816).
states.blackMenRule: The Constitution of 1816 allowed only white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1816, Art. VI, sec. 1 (Indiana Archives and Records Administration)

states.electorMethod: Voters (by districts in 1824; the method in 1828 isn't confirmed).
states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule; men living in the state who weren't citizens could vote too (Constitution of 1818).
states.blackMenRule: The Constitution of 1818 allowed only white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1818, Art. II, sec. 27

states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule (Constitution of 1819).
states.blackMenRule: The Constitution of 1819 allowed only white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1819, Art. III, sec. 5

states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to be enrolled in the militia or have paid a state or county tax (Constitution of 1817).
states.blackMenRule: The Constitution of 1817 allowed only white men.
states.source: Constitution of 1817, Art. III, sec. 1 (Mississippi Department of Archives and History)

states.electorMethod: Voters, statewide, for the first time (the legislature chose until 1824).
states.whiteMen: Had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia)
states.whiteMenRule: Had to have paid a state tax (Constitution of 1812, as historians describe it; some also mention land).
states.blackMenRule: The Constitution of 1812 allowed only free white men.
states.source: 64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities)

states.electorMethod: Voters (by districts in 1824; the method in 1828 isn't confirmed).
states.whiteMenRule: No property or tax rule (Constitution of 1820, as historians describe it).
states.blackMenRule: The Constitution of 1820 allowed only free white men.
states.source: Keyssar, The Right to Vote (tables); Missouri State Parks
